html:
A church in Ravenna begun around 526 under the Ostrogoths and consecrated in 547, after the city had been taken by Belisarius for the eastern empire. It is one of the most important surviving works of early Byzantine art.

The church is an octagon under a dome, with a gallery, like Little Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. A local banker, Julius Argentarius, paid for it. Its glory is the mosaics around the altar. On one side Justinian stands with the bishop Maximian, clergy and soldiers, holding a bowl of bread. Facing him, Theodora in jewels and purple holds a gold cup among her ladies. Neither ever visited Ravenna; the pictures put the far-off rulers in the church.

Charlemagne admired it and modelled his palace chapel at Aachen on it. It is one of eight early Christian buildings in Ravenna listed as a World Heritage Site, with the Mausoleum of Galla Placidia.
